explain.say: You type a website name and press enter, and blink, the page appears. But in that blink, five things happen! Let us slow it down. Look at the first box: you type an address, called a URL, into your browser.

explain.say: Computers find each other by numbers, not names. So the browser asks DNS, which works like a phone book: it turns the name into a number called an IP address. Look at the second box. Why are names easier for you than numbers?

faq.a: DNS, the domain name system, is the internet's phone book. It turns a website name you can remember into the IP address number that computers use to find the server.
asks: How does my browser find a website?

faq.a: A web server is a computer that stores websites and sends the pages to any browser that asks. Big websites use thousands of servers in data centres around the world.
A web browser is the app you use to visit websites, such as Chrome, Safari, Firefox or Edge. It asks servers for pages and turns their HTML code into the page you see.

faq.q: What is the difference between the web and the internet?
faq.a: The internet is the worldwide network of connected computers and cables. The web is one service that runs on it: pages linked together that you view in a browser. Email and video calls also use the internet.
asks: Is the internet the same as the web?

faq.a: HTTPS is the secure way of sending web pages. The data is encrypted, scrambled, so nobody in between can read or change it. Browsers show a padlock when it is used.
asks: What does the padlock in my browser mean?

facts: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989, and the first website went online in 1991.
DNS translates domain names into the IP addresses computers use to locate each other.
